**Part 2: Best Case and Worst Case Time Complexity (4 marks)**

**Best Case: O(n log n)**

Occurs when: The pivot always divides the array into two EQUAL halves.

Recurrence Relation:
```
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
     = O(n log n)
```

Visualization:
```
Level 0: [n elements]                    → n work
Level 1: [n/2 elements] [n/2 elements]  → n work
Level 2: 4 × [n/4 elements]             → n work
...
Level log n: n × [1 element]            → n work

Total: n × log n = O(n log n)
```

When best case occurs:
- Median element chosen as pivot each time
- Random permutation input (on average)
- Randomized pivot selection

**Worst Case: O(n²)**

Occurs when: The pivot is always the smallest or largest element, creating maximally unbalanced partitions.

Recurrence Relation:
```
T(n) = T(n-1) + T(0) + O(n)
     = T(n-1) + O(n)
     = O(n²)
```

Visualization:
```
Level 0: [n elements]           → n work
Level 1: [n-1 elements] [0]     → n-1 work
Level 2: [n-2 elements] [0]     → n-2 work
...
Level n-1: [1 element] [0]      → 1 work

Total: n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²)
```

When worst case occurs:
1. Already sorted array + first or last element as pivot
   - [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with pivot = arr[last] = 5
   - 5 is largest, right partition is empty

2. Reverse sorted array + first element as pivot
   - [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] with pivot = 5
   - Always unbalanced split

**Complexity Summary:**
```
Case         | Condition                    | Time       | Space
-------------+------------------------------+------------+----------
Best Case    | Pivot always at median        | O(n log n) | O(log n)
Average Case | Random input distribution     | O(n log n) | O(log n)
Worst Case   | Pivot always min or max       | O(n²)      | O(n)
```

**How to Avoid Worst Case:**
1. Randomized pivot selection: Choose random element as pivot
2. Median-of-three: Use median of first, middle, last as pivot
3. These reduce worst-case probability to extremely low

**Part 1: Selection Sort with Example (4 marks)**

Definition:
Selection Sort divides the array into a sorted portion (left) and unsorted portion (right). In each pass, it finds the minimum element from the unsorted portion and places it at the start of the unsorted portion.

Algorithm:
```
SelectionSort(arr, n):
    for i = 0 to n-2:
        min_index = i                    // Assume current position is minimum
        
        for j = i+1 to n-1:             // Find minimum in unsorted portion
            if arr[j] < arr[min_index]:
                min_index = j
        
        if min_index ≠ i:               // If minimum found elsewhere
            swap(arr[i], arr[min_index]) // Place minimum in sorted position
```

Step-by-Step Example:

Input: [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]

Pass 1 (i=0): Find minimum in [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]
```
min_index = 0 (arr[0]=29)
j=1: arr[1]=10 < 29 → min_index = 1
j=2: arr[2]=14 > 10 → no change
j=3: arr[3]=37 > 10 → no change
j=4: arr[4]=13 > 10 → no change
Minimum = 10 at index 1
Swap arr[0] and arr[1]

Result: [10, 29, 14, 37, 13]
         ↑ sorted
```

Pass 2 (i=1): Find minimum in [29, 14, 37, 13]
```
min_index = 1 (arr[1]=29)
j=2: arr[2]=14 < 29 → min_index = 2
j=3: arr[3]=37 > 14 → no change
j=4: arr[4]=13 < 14 → min_index = 4
Minimum = 13 at index 4
Swap arr[1] and arr[4]

Result: [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]
             ↑  sorted
```

Pass 3 (i=2): Find minimum in [14, 37, 29]
```
min_index = 2 (arr[2]=14)
j=3: arr[3]=37 > 14 → no change
j=4: arr[4]=29 > 14 → no change
Minimum = 14 already at index 2 — no swap

Result: [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]
                 ↑  sorted
```

Pass 4 (i=3): Find minimum in [37, 29]
```
min_index = 3 (arr[3]=37)
j=4: arr[4]=29 < 37 → min_index = 4
Minimum = 29 at index 4
Swap arr[3] and arr[4]

Result: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37]
                     ↑  sorted
```

Final Sorted Array: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37] ✓

Summary Table:
```
Pass | Array State           | Swap
-----+-----------------------+------------------
 0   | [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]  | original
 1   | [10, 29, 14, 37, 13]  | swap 29 & 10
 2   | [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]  | swap 29 & 13
 3   | [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]  | no swap (14 min)
 4   | [10, 13, 14, 29, 37]  | swap 37 & 29
```

Complexity:
- Time: O(n²) all cases
- Space: O(1) in-place
- Swaps: Maximum n-1 (advantage!)
- Stable: No

---

**Part 2: Comparison of Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort (4 marks)**

```
Property          | Bubble Sort      | Selection Sort   | Insertion Sort
------------------+------------------+------------------+-----------------
Approach          | Repeatedly swap  | Find min, place  | Insert each
                  | adjacent elements| at beginning     | in correct pos.
                  |                  |                  |
Best Case Time    | O(n)             | O(n²)            | O(n)
                  | (optimized)      |                  | (nearly sorted)
                  |                  |                  |
Average Case      | O(n²)            | O(n²)            | O(n²)
                  |                  |                  |
Worst Case Time   | O(n²)            | O(n²)            | O(n²)
                  |                  |                  |
Space Complexity  | O(1)             | O(1)             | O(1)
                  |                  |                  |
In-place          | Yes              | Yes              | Yes
                  |                  |                  |
Stable            | Yes              | No               | Yes
                  |                  |                  |
Adaptive          | Yes (optimized)  | No               | Yes
                  |                  |                  |
Number of Swaps   | O(n²) max        | O(n) max (n-1)   | O(n²) max
                  |                  |                  |
Number of         | O(n²)            | Always O(n²)     | O(n²)
Comparisons       |                  |                  |
                  |                  |                  |
Best For          | Nearly sorted    | Minimizing swaps | Nearly sorted
                  | small data       | small data       | small data
                  |                  |                  |
Worst Input       | Reverse sorted   | All inputs same  | Reverse sorted
```

Key Observations:

1. Selection Sort Unique Advantage:
   - Makes fewest SWAPS (at most n-1)
   - Useful when swap operation is expensive

2. Insertion Sort Unique Advantage:
   - Adaptive: O(n) for already sorted or nearly sorted data
   - Online: Can sort as elements arrive
   - Best choice for small or nearly sorted data

3. Bubble Sort:
   - Simplest to understand
   - With optimization: O(n) for sorted input
   - Generally slowest in practice due to many swaps

4. All Three:
   - O(n²) average/worst case
   - O(1) space complexity
   - Impractical for large datasets (use Merge Sort or Quick Sort)

Practical Use:
- All three used as subroutines in hybrid algorithms (Timsort)
- Insertion sort used for small subarrays in IntroSort
